lesson.title: The Body's Incoming Messengers
lesson.summary: Sensory, or afferent, neurons carry information from receptors throughout the body toward the central nervous system, converting physical stimuli into the electrochemical signals that make sensation and reflexive response possible.
lesson.body:
Every conscious sensation you have, and plenty of unconscious bodily monitoring besides, begins with sensory neurons. Also called afferent neurons, they carry information from receptors throughout the body inward toward the central nervous system. The word afferent is worth remembering precisely because it signals direction: afferent neurons carry signals toward the brain and spinal cord, the opposite direction from the motor neurons discussed next.

Structurally, sensory neurons are built for detection and long-distance transmission. Many have specialized dendritic endings embedded in the skin, muscles, joints, or sensory organs, shaped to respond to a particular kind of stimulus. From there, a long axon carries the resulting signal, often over a considerable distance, into the spinal cord or directly into the brainstem, entering the central nervous system through the dorsal, or back-facing, side of the spinal cord. The cell bodies of many sensory neurons cluster together just outside the spinal cord in structures called dorsal root ganglia, small swellings along each spinal nerve where the incoming sensory fibers are gathered before their signals continue into the cord itself.

Different sensory neurons are tuned to different kinds of information. Some respond to light touch or pressure on the skin, others to changes in temperature, others specifically to tissue damage in the form of pain, and still others to the position and movement of joints and muscles, a sense called proprioception that lets you know where your limbs are without looking at them. Specialized sensory neurons in the eyes and ears handle light and sound, feeding that information into the same general afferent pathway toward the brain. This same afferent design explains proprioception: sensory neurons embedded in your muscles and joints continuously report tension and position back to the spinal cord and brain, which is how you can touch your nose with a finger even with your eyes closed.

Consider again the example of touching a hot stove. The instant your skin contacts the heat, sensory neurons in your fingertips convert that thermal and painful stimulus into an electrochemical signal and carry it along their axons into your spinal cord. From there the signal can trigger a fast local reflex while a parallel copy continues upward to the brain, where it is finally registered as the conscious experience of pain.

Sensory neurons matter functionally because an organism that cannot detect what is happening to its body and environment cannot respond appropriately to it. They supply the raw input that interneurons process and that motor neurons ultimately act on, making them the essential first step in nearly every behavior, reflexive or deliberate, described elsewhere in this unit. This is also why certain nerve conditions, such as the peripheral neuropathy that can accompany long-standing diabetes, tend to appear first as numbness or tingling in the feet and hands, since those areas depend on some of the longest sensory axons in the body.
